title: Dirichlet Characters L Functions and Primes in Progressions

items.title: Dirichlet characters modulo q
Extension by zero is well defined and periodic
items.strategy: Check that unit status and the value of the underlying group homomorphism depend only on the residue class modulo q. Then the zero extension is representative-independent, q-periodic, and vanishes exactly on nonunits.

items.title: Arithmetic characterization of Dirichlet characters modulo q
items.strategy: For the forward direction, read periodicity, complete multiplicativity, and the coprimality support from the zero-extension definition. For the converse, restrict the arithmetic function to unit classes modulo q, prove that restriction is a well-defined homomorphism, and then recover the original function by extension by zero.

items.title: The principal character modulo q
Character values on units are roots of unity
items.strategy: For a unit class a, apply the character to a suitable positive power equal to the identity in the finite unit group to force chi(a) to be a root of unity. Complex conjugation is then inversion on unit values, while both sides are zero on nonunits by the extension convention.

items.title: Orthogonality relations for Dirichlet characters modulo q
items.strategy: Identify Dirichlet characters modulo q with one-dimensional complex characters of the finite abelian group (Z/qZ)^x. Use the published finite-group orthogonality relations together with the fact that every irreducible character of a finite abelian group has degree one and that there are exactly phi(q) of them.

items.title: A residue-class indicator from character sums
items.strategy: Apply the column orthogonality relation to the unit group element represented by a and to the residue class of n when n is coprime to q. The extension-by-zero convention makes the same sum vanish automatically when n shares a prime factor with q.

items.title: A nonprincipal character has zero complete sum
items.strategy: Let S be the sum over one complete residue system modulo q. Multiply S by chi(a) for a unit with chi(a) not equal to 1, then reindex the residue classes by multiplication by a to obtain the same sum. The scalar factor forces S to be zero.

items.title: Nonprincipal Dirichlet character partial sums are bounded
items.strategy: Break the first x terms into complete blocks of length q together with one terminal block. Every complete block vanishes by the previous lemma, and the leftover block has at most q terms of modulus at most one.

items.title: Dirichlet L-functions
Euler product for Dirichlet L-functions
items.strategy: View the Dirichlet character as a completely multiplicative coefficient function of modulus at most one. In the absolute half-plane Re(s) greater than 1, invoke the published Euler-product theorem for completely multiplicative Dirichlet series and then apply the usual logarithmic expansion to show the product is nonzero there.

items.title: The principal Dirichlet L-function factors through zeta
items.strategy: Compare Euler products prime by prime: the principal character agrees with 1 away from primes dividing q and vanishes at those bad primes. This removes exactly the finitely many Euler factors dividing q and transfers zeta's simple pole and residue formula to L(s, chi_0).

items.title: Nonprincipal Dirichlet L-functions are holomorphic on Re s greater than 0
items.strategy: Use the bounded partial sums of a nonprincipal character inside the published summatory-integral formula for Dirichlet series. The integral converges locally uniformly on every half-plane Re(s) at least epsilon greater than 0, yielding holomorphy there.

items.title: Positive logarithmic Dirichlet series force boundary nonvanishing
items.strategy: Package the logarithm of the relevant Euler product as a Dirichlet series with nonnegative coefficients and apply Landau's theorem only on the real axis. The contradiction comes from trying to continue a finite boundary value past the abscissa where the source series would have to diverge unless a pole accounts for it.

items.title: The full product of Dirichlet L-functions has no zero on Re s = 1
items.strategy: Sum the logarithmic Euler products of all Dirichlet L-functions modulo q and use character orthogonality to group the coefficients into nonnegative prime blocks. Landau's theorem then rules out zeros at regular points of Re(s)=1, and the pole at s=1 is handled by an explicit meromorphic order count using the principal factorization.

items.title: Nonprincipal Dirichlet L-functions do not vanish on Re s = 1 away from s = 1
items.strategy: If a nonprincipal factor vanished at 1+it with t nonzero, the finite product over all characters would vanish there as well. The previous theorem excludes that, so every nonprincipal factor stays nonzero at those points.

items.title: A nonreal Dirichlet L-function is nonzero at one
items.strategy: A zero of L(1, chi) for a nonreal character forces the conjugate character to vanish there as well. Their combined order would then overwhelm the single principal pole inside the full finite product, contradicting the line-one product theorem.

items.title: A real nonprincipal Dirichlet L-function is nonzero at one
items.strategy: Assume a zero at s=1 and build the source's auxiliary Euler product with nonnegative coefficients from the principal factor and the real character factor. Continue that product to a right half-plane using the earlier holomorphy statements, then apply the positive-coefficient Landau argument against the explicit lower bound coming from its constant term.

items.title: Nonprincipal Dirichlet L-functions are nonzero at one
items.strategy: Split into the disjoint real and nonreal cases and invoke the two preceding lemmas.

items.title: Natural and Dirichlet density
Natural density implies Dirichlet density
items.strategy: Write the Dirichlet series of the indicator function by summatory integration against the counting function of the set. Replacing that counting function by its natural-density main term plus an error yields the claimed logarithmic asymptotic as s decreases to 1.

items.title: Primes in one reduced residue class have Dirichlet density 1 over phi(q)
items.strategy: Take logarithms of L(s, chi) for s greater than 1, separate prime terms from prime-power terms, and average against the conjugate character values of the target residue class. Orthogonality isolates the desired prime sum, while the principal character supplies the only logarithmic singularity because every nonprincipal L(1, chi) is nonzero.

items.title: Mertens sum for primes in an arithmetic progression
items.strategy: Average the weighted prime sums over Dirichlet characters: the principal character contributes log x by the ordinary first Mertens theorem, the nonprincipal weighted sums stay bounded because -L'/L is regular at s=1, and Abel summation converts that to the reciprocal-prime asymptotic.

items.title: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
items.strategy: The asymptotic from the preceding theorem forces the reciprocal sum over primes in the progression to diverge like (1/phi(q)) log log x. A finite set of primes could not produce that divergence, so infinitely many primes lie in the progression.

title: Dirichlet Characters L Functions and Primes in Progressions -- Examples

items.title: Dirichlet character tables modulo 3, 4, and 5
items.strategy: List the units modulo each modulus, write every group homomorphism from the unit group to roots of unity, and then extend each table by zero on nonunits.

items.title: Dirichlet character tables modulo 8 and 12
items.strategy: Use the product structure of the unit groups to write all homomorphisms explicitly. Record the resulting values on every residue class so the extension-by-zero convention stays visible.

items.title: An orthogonality table for Dirichlet characters
items.strategy: Choose a small modulus, compute the complete character table, and verify both orthogonality sums and the residue-class indicator directly by finite arithmetic.

items.title: Missing Euler factors for a principal Dirichlet L-function
items.strategy: Compute the principal character Euler product for two small moduli and compare it termwise with zeta. Then read off the residue at s=1 from the finite bad-prime factor.

items.title: The character chi_4 and the Gregory-Leibniz series
items.strategy: Use the nonprincipal holomorphic-continuation theorem to identify L(1, chi_4) with its convergent Dirichlet series, then substitute the explicit values of chi_4 and invoke the published Gregory-Leibniz theorem.

items.title: Dirichlet density for a small prime progression
items.strategy: Pick a reduced class modulo a small q, compute the character average that singles it out, and explain how the theorem predicts the coefficient of the logarithmic divergence without treating the finite data as evidence of proof.

items.title: A noncoprime residue class has no Dirichlet conclusion
items.strategy: If gcd(a, q) is greater than 1, then every number congruent to a modulo q shares that divisor, except possibly the prime equal to the divisor itself. Work out a concrete modulus and residue class to show why the coprimality hypothesis is indispensable.

items.title: Positive prime Dirichlet density does not give positive integer natural density
items.strategy: Compare the prime-counting function in one residue class with the ambient counting function of all integers. The class has positive relative density among primes but still density zero among positive integers because pi(x) grows much more slowly than x.

title: Hilbert Symbols and the Quadratic Local Global Principle

items.title: The rational local fields
The Hilbert symbol over a rational completion
Equivalent formulations of the Hilbert symbol
items.strategy: Translate the equation ax^2 + by^2 = 1 into isotropy of a ternary diagonal form by homogenizing, then into a binary representation statement by solving for one variable. For the norm formulation, expand N(x + y sqrt(a)) = x^2 - ay^2 and track the sign change explicitly.

items.title: The Hilbert symbol depends only on square classes
items.strategy: Rescale variables by square roots in one direction and by their inverses in the other. This gives a direct equivalence between solvability for (a, b)_v and solvability for (au^2, bv^2)_v.

items.title: The real Hilbert symbol formula
items.strategy: If one coefficient is positive, solve immediately by taking the other variable zero. If both are negative, the defining equation would write 1 as a sum of two nonpositive real numbers and is therefore impossible.

items.title: The odd-prime Hilbert symbol formula
items.strategy: Use square-class invariance to reduce a and b to valuation parity and unit residues. The four resulting cases are settled by the odd-p square criterion and the Legendre symbol conventions already fixed on the quadratic-residue pages.

items.title: The two-adic Hilbert symbol formula
items.strategy: Reduce to valuation parity together with odd unit classes modulo eight. The explicit exponent formula is then a finite check on the eight square classes, using the exact Q_2 square criterion rather than any heuristic sign argument.

items.title: The Hilbert symbol is a symmetric bilinear nondegenerate pairing
items.strategy: Symmetry is evident from the defining equation. Bilinearity can be checked either through the norm criterion or directly on the finite square-class representatives supplied by the local formulas, and nondegeneracy is proved by producing, for each nontrivial square class, an explicit witness class detected by one of those formulas.

items.title: Binary quadratic representation via the Hilbert symbol
items.strategy: Rewrite the claim that aX^2 + bY^2 represents t as isotropy of aX^2 + bY^2 - tZ^2. Apply the equivalent norm formulation and then use bilinearity to move t and -ab to the opposite side of the Hilbert-symbol identity.

items.title: Ternary isotropy via the Hilbert symbol
items.strategy: Move one diagonal term to the other side and apply the binary representation lemma to the remaining two-variable form. Track the minus signs explicitly so the criterion matches the chosen normalization of the Hilbert symbol.

items.title: Quadratic forms of dimension at least three over odd finite fields are isotropic
items.strategy: Diagonalize the form, then count square values in the finite field using that the multiplicative group is cyclic. For fixed nonzero c, the value sets of ax^2 and -c - by^2 each have more than half the field's elements, so they intersect and produce a nontrivial zero with the third coordinate equal to 1.

items.title: Almost all local completions are isotropic in dimension at least three
items.strategy: After diagonalizing and clearing denominators, exclude finitely many primes dividing 2 or the diagonal coefficients. Over every remaining residue field the reduced ternary-or-higher form is isotropic by the finite-field lemma, and a nonsingular zero lifts to Q_p by the p-adic root-lifting theorem.

items.title: Hilbert reciprocity over the rationals
items.strategy: Use bilinearity to reduce to the generator classes -1, 2, and odd primes. The local formulas then check the diagonal and exceptional pairs directly and reduce the remaining products to quadratic reciprocity and its two supplements.

items.title: One local place is determined by the others for ternary forms
items.strategy: Multiply the local ternary isotropy criterion over all places and apply Hilbert reciprocity to the right-hand side. If every factor except one is known to be 1, the remaining factor must also be 1.

items.title: Hasse-Minkowski for ternary forms over Q
items.strategy: Reduce to Z^2-aX^2-bY^2 with squarefree a and b and descend on |a|+|b|. Local norm identities produce a smaller locally isotropic ternary form, and a norm-division argument lifts a rational zero of the smaller form back to the original one.

items.title: Global approximation of finitely many square classes
items.strategy: Use weak approximation to realize the prescribed local square classes, then multiply by a correction factor M/ell where Dirichlet chooses ell so the local classes stay fixed while every outside valuation becomes even except possibly at ell.

items.title: Hasse-Minkowski theorem over Q
items.strategy: Diagonalize and induct on dimension. Dimension four is handled by patching one global square class and applying the ternary theorem to two auxiliary ternary forms, while higher dimensions use local isotropy of the tail subform outside finitely many places and weak approximation to match the first binary value.

title: Hilbert Symbols and the Quadratic Local Global Principle -- Examples

items.title: Hilbert symbols over the real numbers
items.strategy: Work through all sign combinations of a and b and compare the solvability test with the norm interpretation from the quadratic extension R(sqrt(a)).

items.title: A Hilbert-symbol computation at an odd prime
items.strategy: Write the inputs as p-adic valuation parts times units, reduce to parity data and Legendre symbols, and then substitute into the explicit odd-prime formula.

items.title: The two-adic Hilbert symbol table
items.strategy: Reduce to the square classes of odd units modulo eight and valuation parity, then evaluate the exponent formula case by case.

items.title: A local obstruction to a rational conic
items.strategy: Choose a diagonal ternary form for which one completion gives the wrong Hilbert-symbol value. The local failure blocks isotropy there and therefore blocks rational points over Q as well.

items.title: Finite bad places for a ternary form
items.strategy: Identify the finitely many primes dividing 2 or the diagonal coefficients, compute the local symbols only at those places, and explain why all remaining primes are automatically good.

items.title: The one-place principle in action
items.strategy: Compute the local Hilbert-symbol values of a ternary form at all but one completion, multiply them, and use reciprocity to infer the missing one.

items.title: A quaternary Hasse-Minkowski calculation
items.strategy: Carry out the dimension-four patching step explicitly: match the required local square classes, build the global scalar, and reduce the problem to a ternary isotropy check.

items.title: Selmer's cubic is locally soluble but globally insoluble
items.strategy: Use the sourced Selmer example 3x^3 + 4y^3 + 5z^3 = 0. Record the real and p-adic solutions by the source's Hensel-lifting cases, then cite the source's later algebraic-number-theory argument for the absence of nontrivial rational solutions without importing its out-of-scope machinery.

items.title: Rational isotropy does not solve an integral representation problem
items.strategy: Contrast a homogenized rational-isotropy statement with a fixed integral equation. Clearing denominators changes the represented number, so the local-global theorem for isotropy does not decide the original integral representation question.
